source: Netball Skills and Conditioning Manual, Level 1, 3rd version, Niel du Plessis and Erin Burger, Passing section, page 81, heading '1 HAND HIGH PASS' at manual line 2670. Three numbered steps at 2672, 2673 and 2674, and four warnings at 2676.
notes: THE LIBRARY'S FIRST ONE-HANDED PASS. She has the ball from frame 0, lifts it on the right arm as high as that arm goes, steps, and releases at 0.80. The two existing one-handed drills are catches; this is the first that sends the ball away with one hand.
handsNote: RIGHT, NOT BOTH, AND THIS IS THE CHOICE THAT SHAPES EVERY OTHER FILE. The manual heads the block '1 HAND HIGH PASS' and its cue 3 is singular: 'Keep hand behind the ball'. Right follows netball_hooks_outside_hand and netball_one_hand_snatch_to_other_hand, the library's only other one-handed drills, both of which are hands='right'. THE CONSEQUENCE IS STRUCTURAL: technique.carries_no_side() returns False on its first line for anything but 'both', so this drill is UNEVEN BY CONSTRUCTION and can never enter the even population that the knee-mirror guards read. That is correct rather than a defect, and it is asserted by name in test_waiting_hand.py's named-uneven list rather than left to be inferred.
turnNote: false. Nothing arrives, so there is nothing to turn toward. She is already facing where she is passing.

grip.note: The library's measured 90 degrees, carried unchanged from the other passes. PROVISIONAL FOR A ONE-HANDED OVERHEAD HOLD, and more provisional here than anywhere it has been used. The 90 was measured for a two-handed catch at the chest, where the hands take the sides of the ball and the thumbs meet behind its middle. ONE HAND CANNOT DO THAT: there is no second hand to meet, so the geometry the number was derived from is not the geometry it is spent in. This is the fault class docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md calls a constant calibrated in one regime and spent in another, and it is recorded here rather than corrected, because correcting it needs a coach or a photograph and this lane has neither.

releaseNote: Anchored at the frame the hand comes off the ball, with the follow-through graded as its own phase. The pattern netball_chest_pass established and the other two passes follow. 0.80 also matches the manual's warning 'Don't wait too long to release', which is the only cue in this block about WHEN.

afterContact.name: held
afterContact.note: The ball at her chest on the first frame, the same place the other three passes start. REDUNDANT and kept for readability: the ball track's first key governs the pose at frame 0, which netball_overhead_pass's mutation work proved.

afterContact.name: lift
afterContact.note: The manual's step 1, 'Pull the ball up as high as arm can go' (line 2672). TWO THINGS DISTINGUISH THIS FROM netball_overhead_pass'S LIFT, and both are deliberate. It is HIGHER: 1.42 torso lengths against 1.12, aimed at the reach limit rather than at head height, because the manual's word is 'as high as arm can go' and the overhead pass's is 'above your head'. And it is OFF THE MIDLINE: across -0.20 puts the ball over the throwing shoulder rather than over her head, because one arm cannot hold a ball on the centre line above the crown without the trunk twisting under it. The right shoulder sits at -0.3818 torso lengths, so -0.20 is about half way out. WHAT HEIGHT THIS ACTUALLY REACHES IS MEASURED IN THE DEFINITION'S reachNote, and it is NOT what this number asks for.

afterContact.name: step
afterContact.note: The manual's step 2 begins, 'Give a small step'. The ball stays high and comes forward. The step itself is in the motion file's root travel; it has NO MEASURE and is recorded as a gap.

afterContact.name: release
afterContact.note: The last frame the hand is on the ball. The ball has come forward and slightly down off the peak and back toward the midline, which is what an arm throwing through the ball does. AHEAD IS 0.96 AND A FIRST DRAFT USED 0.78, WHICH SAT IN A SOLVER BASIN 0.03 TORSO LENGTHS WIDE. Mapping this key from 0.90 down to 0.70 found four basins separated by pose jumps of 18 to 20 cm: 0.90 to 0.80 is one smooth region with joint steps of 0.67 to 0.72 cm, then 0.79 to 0.76 is a different solution entered with a 19.85 cm jump, and 0.74 and 0.72 are two more. The first draft's 0.78 was inside the narrow one, and THREE graded readings moved with it: the release elbow 49.68 against 65.29, the release shoulder 112.01 against 133.58 and the follow-through shoulder 86.63 against 102.47. 0.96 is deep inside the wide basin, which runs unbroken from 0.80 to at least 1.34, and it matches netball_bounce_pass's release carry exactly. Refer to the definition's basinNote.

carryUnitNote: afterContact is measured in torso lengths, not arm lengths. Where a ball sits relative to the body depends on the body and the ball, not on how long the arm is. Every number here was multiplied by 1.017053, the reference athlete's arm over her torso, so her positions are unchanged and only other bodies change. THE LIFT KEY IS THE ONE PLACE THIS CONVENTION IS UNCOMFORTABLE: 'as high as ARM can go' is the one cue in this library that genuinely depends on arm length, and it is authored in torso lengths like its neighbours. Refer to the definition's reachNote.
